extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory; readers studying Montesquieu and classical government theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition and critique of Montesquieu's classification of governments (republic, monarchy, despotism), their constitutive and conservative principles, and the modes by which each form becomes corrupt. Emphasizes conceptual distinctions useful for evaluating or constructing taxonomies of regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish constitutive vs conservator principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A government has (1) a principle that makes it be (constitutive) and (2) a principle that makes it last (conservator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify both what constitutes a form of government (e.g., distribution of sovereignty, love of liberty/rest) and what sustains it over time (virtue, honor, fear, moderation). Use both axes to explain why a regime exists and why it endures or decays. (Text: 'Il y a deux principes... l'un le fait être, l'autre le fait durer.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic (constitutive) — virtue as principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutive principle of the republic is virtue — specifically 'l'amour de la patrie', understood as love of equality (a political virtue, distinct from moral or Christian virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating republican regimes, ask whether citizens possess the political virtue (esteem for equality and the public good). Distinguish political virtue from private moral virtue and note that republics require this public-spiritedness to function. (Quotes and explanation drawn from Montesquieu and the commentator.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy vs aristocracy distinction (distribution of sovereignty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate democracy (sovereignty in the whole people) from aristocracy (sovereignty in a part/the great), because distribution of sovereignty (one, several, all) fundamentally changes the spirit of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification should treat 'several' as a distinct category from 'all' and 'one' — do not conflate democratic and aristocratic forms simply because neither is monarchical. The commentator criticizes mixing different dividing principles (number of rulers vs obedience to law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy (conservative principle) — moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu identifies moderation as the virtue proper and the principle of aristocracy: nobles must restrain passions and maintain equality with themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'moderation' to evaluate aristocratic regimes insofar as nobles exercise self-restraint and regard themselves as equals of the people; but note the critique that moderation is a limiting condition rather than a positive principle of action (it prevents loss but does not generate motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy (conservative principle) — honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu claims the conservator principle of monarchy is 'honor' — the set of prejudices of each person and condition that make individuals seek distinctions and respect traditional ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether 'honor' (understood as regard for rank, self-regard, and limits on obedience) operates to bind prince and subjects. The commentator emphasizes the vagueness of 'honor' and distinguishes honor-as-vanity from honor-as-fidelity-to-conscience; clarify which sense is meant when applying the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism (constitutive/conservative principle) — fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism rests solely on the fear of the sovereign; it possesses no determinate constitution and no sustaining principles beyond terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect despotism by the predominance of fear as the mechanism of rule and by absence of intermediate powers or law-based limits. Note the critique that a regime based only on fear is internally contradictory (peace requires security, which fear undermines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate powers and institutional buffers in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarchy requires, alongside the prince, subordinate/ intermediate powers (nobility, clergy, municipal jurisdictions, etc.) and a deposit of laws and agents who promulgate and recall laws; these limit arbitrary power by creating channels of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate monarchies by presence and strength of intermediate bodies that constrain the prince and institutional mechanisms (legal customs, bodies that announce/recall laws). Their absence signals drift toward despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as a conservator in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: In a monarchy, 'opinion' (a public sense that the sovereign owes his power to the subjects' good) functions as a check: the monarch may be legally supreme but in fact must reckon with opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent and force of public opinion and its ability to approve or blame acts and ministers; stronger opinion indicates a monarchy leaning away from despotism and toward liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological consistency in classifying governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix dividing principles: either divide governments by distribution of sovereignty (one, several, all) or by whether they obey law (law-obedient vs lawless) and then subdivide; mixing both leads to incoherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing a taxonomy, choose a single primary axis (e.g., number of rulers OR obedience to law). The commentator suggests Aristotle's approach (good/bad forms) or first classifying by obedience to law then by number as consistent alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience-to-law as alternative classification axis
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative sound division: first split governments by whether they obey laws (those that do vs those that do not), then subdivide each class into one/several/all — yielding six forms (three good, three corrupt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obedience-to-law as a primary principle when laws vs caprice matters for the analysis; it captures the distinction between legitimate monarchy and despotic caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption begins with corruption of the principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The corruption of each government starts with the corruption of its foundational principle (e.g., republic loses virtue; monarchy loses honor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To diagnose decay, identify which core principle has degenerated and trace how that leads to institutional and moral decline. The commentator repeatedly emphasizes this as the starting point for regime collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy corruption modes — loss or exaggeration of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy is corrupted either by loss of the spirit of equality (leading towards oligarchy/aristocracy) or by exaggerated equality (leading first to general despotism and then to single-person tyranny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate democratic corruption by checking whether equality is being undermined (privilege) or distorted into extremes (equalization of magistrates, judges, fathers, masters) that dissolve lawful distinctions and produce anarchy or concentrated tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires civic virtue/justice to endure
rubrics_metrics.description: Because democracy grants extensive liberty, it can only last if the people possess virtue (justice, obedience to laws, respect for magistrates and elders); otherwise liberty becomes anarchy and self-destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess civic education, prevalence of public-spirited behavior, respect for law and magistrates; modern democracies may substitute economic concerns but still need justice as their sustaining principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy corruption modes
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy corrupts when the nobility separates from the people, commands by will rather than law, concentrates or relaxes power into tyranny or weakness, or when nobles prefer command's delights to its perils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for social separation between elites and people, erosion of legal restraint on nobles, and the nobles' loss of sense of duty; these signal transition toward tyrannical or ineffectual rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy corruption modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy decays when honor transforms into servitude, when obedience becomes mere instrumentality, when honors contradict actual dignity (infamy with dignities), when monarch rules by will instead of law, when intermediate powers are suppressed and the prince seeks all action himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect erosion by observing whether legal limits and intermediate bodies are being removed, whether the prince substitutes personal caprice for law, and whether honor now masks subservience rather than restraining power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism is an abusive form of monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentator argues despotism is not essentially distinct but is an abusive or degraded form of monarchy where sovereignty is unlimited and rule rests on caprice and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing regimes, consider despotism as a degeneration of monarchy rather than a wholly separate ideal type; check for extreme concentration of power, absence of durable customs, and reliance on terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'moderation' as a principal motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation is criticized as a weak principle: it is a limit preventing loss, not a principle that moves government; it is necessary for all governments and thus not specific to aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating moderation as an explanatory motor of aristocratic government; instead treat it as a general desideratum for regime stability applicable across forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify 'honor' — distinguish vanity, aristocratic honor, and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of honor is ambiguous: it can mean vanity/preference for distinctions, aristocratic prejudices, or a form of virtue (self-respect that limits obedience). The proper political meaning must be specified when used as a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'honor' to analyze monarchies, specify which sense is operative (narrow aristocratic prejudice vs broader civic virtue). The commentator suggests the most distinctive monarchic sense is the pride that refuses commands contrary to conscience — a limit on the prince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two natural human principles that generate principal regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two natural principles in men give rise to the two main constitutions: love of repose (giving rise to monarchy) and love of liberty (giving rise to democracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use psychological/social predispositions (preference for rest/order vs preference for movement/freedom) as explanatory variables when assessing why particular societies tend toward monarchy or democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical caution about absolute categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Real governments are often mixtures and practical transactions between pure forms; absolute categories (pure monarchy vs pure despotism) are rare in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical regimes, allow for mixed forms and pragmatic hybrids (parliamentary, representative, limited monarchy) rather than forcing them into strict pure categories.
